pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Reflecting Light

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 3 Science, Light):** notice that light is reflected from surfaces.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary reflection performance expectation. The nearest is 1-PS4-3 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-3]' — materials include reflective ones such as a mirror; the DCI notes '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-3]'; assessment boundary excludes the speed of light); a grade band later, 4-PS4-2 uses reflected light entering the eye to explain seeing.

- **Operational details:** The core idea is that light bounces off surfaces — and the single most important design decision is to investigate BOTH shiny AND dull/matt objects. The 'only shiny things reflect' misconception is largely INSTRUCTION-INDUCED: if every reflection example is a mirror, children conclude only mirrors reflect. So establish 'light bounces' with a mirror first (clean, predictable redirection of a torch beam), then deliberately extend to rough/diffuse surfaces (paper, foil, the wall) to show all surfaces reflect light to different degrees. Connect reflection to SEEING — we see non-luminous objects because they reflect light to the eye — which sets up 'How We See Objects' later. Use hands-on, repeated, darkened-room beam activities and a 'can it reflect light?' sort; expect resistance and re-test. Avoid the misleading 'the Moon reflects like a mirror' analogy (it reflects, but diffusely, like a giant rock).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 7–8 success is the concrete observation that light bounces off surfaces and that smooth shiny surfaces reflect it best/most clearly. The threshold is widening 'reflection' beyond mirrors — noticing that dull surfaces reflect too (just scattered) — and beginning to link reflection to why we can see things. Mastery is observational, not the law of reflection (angle in = angle out), which is formalised later.
bestPractices: Deliberately investigate BOTH shiny and dull/matt surfaces — restricting examples to mirrors is what breeds the 'only shiny things reflect' misconception.
Establish 'light bounces' with a plane mirror first (clean, predictable beam redirection), then extend to rough/diffuse surfaces to show every surface reflects light to some degree.
Connect reflection to seeing: we see non-luminous objects because they reflect light to our eyes — setting up 'How We See Objects'.
Use hands-on, darkened-room torch-beam activities and a 'can it reflect light?' sort; provide repeated experiences and expect the idea to be resistant, so re-test.
Use a formative probe to surface whether children still believe only shiny surfaces reflect, before and after teaching.
Avoid misleading analogies such as 'the Moon reflects like a mirror' — it reflects diffusely, like a giant rock, not as an image-forming mirror.
keyRepresentations: A torch beam bouncing off an angled mirror onto a target or wall (clean redirection)
Side-by-side beam comparison: mirror vs foil vs matt paper vs black card (clean bounce vs scatter)
A 'can it reflect light?' classification sort of everyday objects
A mirror used to redirect a beam around a corner / a simple periscope
Reflection linked to a simple source→object→eye sketch (why we see the object)
commonMisconceptions: Only shiny surfaces (mirrors) reflect light; dull or dark surfaces don't reflect at all.
An object either absorbs OR reflects light — it cannot do both.
Reflection (and the law of reflection) only happens with mirrors.
Black objects reflect no light whatsoever.
The Moon reflects light 'like a mirror' (forming an image) rather than diffusely.
Reflection is unrelated to everyday seeing — a special mirror effect rather than how we see all objects.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, teach that light bounces off surfaces (reflection) by aiming a torch beam in a darkened space, first establishing clean redirection with a plane mirror, then deliberately extending to rough or dull/matt surfaces (paper, crumpled foil, a wall, black card) to show every surface reflects light to some degree — just scattered. Link reflection to seeing: we see non-luminous objects because light bounces off them into our eyes. The central correction is widening 'reflection' beyond mirrors, countering the instruction-induced 'only shiny things reflect' misconception. Mastery here is observational, not the formal law of reflection (angle in = angle out), which comes later.

activities.title: Bounce the beam onto a target with a mirror
feedback: If the beam reaches the target, point out that the light didn't stop at the mirror — it bounced off and carried on in a new direction.
If the learner struggles to aim, note that changing the mirror angle changes where the reflected beam lands, so reflection has a predictable direction.
If the learner steers the beam around a corner, point out that a mirror can redirect light to a place the torch could not reach directly — that is how a periscope works.
Name the clean single bright spot as the mark of a smooth shiny surface reflecting light neatly.
activities.rationale: Starting with a plane mirror gives a clean, predictable demonstration that light bounces before the harder idea that dull surfaces reflect too, matching the recommended teaching sequence. A live, steerable beam makes the redirection concrete; an optional target to hit, an adjustable mirror angle, and an around-a-corner/periscope extension make the mechanism visible.
sourceClaims: IOP recommends starting reflection teaching with plane mirrors to establish that light bounces, then extending to diffuse reflection from irregular surfaces, and explicitly avoiding restricting examples to shiny surfaces; reflection should be linked to seeing non-luminous objects.

NGSS 1-PS4-3 investigates [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-3], including reflective materials such as a mirror, and the DCI states '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-PS4-3]' with assessment excluding the speed of light; there is no dedicated elementary reflection PE.
learnerActions: In a darkened space, use a torch and an angled plane mirror to bounce the beam onto a chosen target or wall spot (aim at the target or wall, not into anyone's eyes).
Adjust the mirror's angle and watch the bright spot move, learning that light can be redirected.
As an optional extension, use the mirror (or two mirrors) to steer the beam around a corner to a hidden spot, like a simple periscope.
Describe in your own words what the mirror does to the beam (it bounces/redirects the light cleanly).
activities.intendedInsight: Light travels in a beam and bounces off a smooth mirror in a clean, predictable way — this is reflection.

activities.title: Swap the mirror for dull surfaces and compare the bounce
feedback: When a faint glow still reaches the target from the dull or dark surface, highlight that the dull surface reflected light too — just messily/scattered, not in a neat beam.

If the learner expected nothing from the wall or black card, treat the surprise as the key moment: light still bounced, so dull surfaces reflect as well; note that a very dark surface returns only a little light, so look carefully — how much it returns depends on the material.
Contrast the clean single spot (mirror) with the spread-out faint glow (matt) to distinguish clear reflection from scattered reflection, without claiming dull surfaces reflect nothing.
If the learner says a surface 'only absorbs' light, note that surfaces usually do both — they absorb some and reflect some; even a dark surface scatters a little back.
activities.rationale: The misconception is largely instruction-induced by only ever using mirror examples, so deliberately investigating both shiny AND dull surfaces is the corrective. Seeing a clean spot change into a scattered glow, and predicting before each surface is placed in the beam, make the comparison concrete; this idea is resistant, so repeated hands-on experience matters. How much light a dull/black surface returns depends on the material and setup, so it is framed as an observation to test, not a guaranteed result.
sourceClaims: Common misconception that light is only reflected from shiny surfaces (e.g. mirrors) and that an object must either absorb OR reflect; the correct concept is that all objects absorb and reflect light to different degrees; the misconception is partly instruction-induced (always using mirror examples), so include shiny AND dull objects; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated activities and is resistant.

IOP recommends starting reflection teaching with plane mirrors to establish that light bounces, then extending to diffuse reflection from irregular surfaces, and explicitly avoiding restricting examples to shiny surfaces; reflection should be linked to seeing non-luminous objects.
learnerActions: Replace the mirror with crumpled foil, matt card, plain wall, then black card, aiming the torch at each in turn.
Watch whether the neat bright spot from the mirror breaks up into scattered light on the other surfaces: a soft, spread-out glow from matt ones, and many small glints from crumpled foil.
Predict before the black/dull wall swap whether any light will reach the target, then test and observe whether a faint reflected glow still lands.
Compare side by side: mirror vs foil vs matt paper vs black card, noting clean bounce versus scatter.
activities.intendedInsight: All surfaces reflect at least some light; smooth shiny surfaces reflect it most cleanly, while dull rough surfaces scatter it — so it isn't 'only shiny things reflect'.

activities.title: Sort surfaces by how well they reflect, and link to seeing
feedback: If a learner tries to make a 'reflects nothing' group and puts dull objects in it, ask whether they can see that object — if yes, then light must have bounced off it to their eyes, so it belongs in 'reflects but scatters it'.
Reinforce that shiny smooth surfaces belong with 'reflects best/most neatly', not 'the only things that reflect'.
Connect the source→object→eye sketch to everyday seeing so reflection is not treated as a special mirror-only effect.
activities.rationale: A sort can consolidate the bounce-and-compare experience and check classification, and the 'you can see it, so light bounced off it' reasoning bridges to How We See Objects. Categorising and a source→object→eye sketch make the link explicit; a sort checks the conclusion and classification but does not itself elicit the physical beam-handling, so it follows the beam work rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: IOP recommends starting reflection teaching with plane mirrors to establish that light bounces, then extending to diffuse reflection from irregular surfaces, and explicitly avoiding restricting examples to shiny surfaces; reflection should be linked to seeing non-luminous objects.

Common misconception that light is only reflected from shiny surfaces (e.g. mirrors) and that an object must either absorb OR reflect; the correct concept is that all objects absorb and reflect light to different degrees; the misconception is partly instruction-induced (always using mirror examples), so include shiny AND dull objects; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated activities and is resistant.
learnerActions: Classify a set of everyday objects by how well each reflects light — a 'reflects best/most neatly' group (smooth shiny surfaces) and a 'reflects but scatters it' group (dull/rough surfaces) — in a 'can it reflect light?' sort, noticing that every object reflects at least some light, so the sort compares degree rather than presence of reflection.
For a dull object you can still see, trace where the light comes from: source → object → eye, and explain that you see it because light bounced off it into your eyes.
Give everyday reflection examples such as a mirror, a puddle, or a polished floor.
activities.intendedInsight: Reflection is how we see non-luminous objects: even a dull surface sends some light to our eyes, which is the only reason we can see it.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: does a dull black surface reflect?
feedback: If the prediction is 'no light bounces off', ask: if the dull paper reflected no light at all, could you see its surface in the dark room with just the torch shining on it? If you can see the paper's surface (not just a dark shape against a lit background), some light did bounce off it.
Prompt the contrast: what's different about the way light bounces off a smooth mirror compared with the rough paper? (clean beam vs scatter).
Ask the learner to name something dull they can see right now and say where the light reaching their eyes comes from.
If a learner says we see the paper 'because it's black', redirect to: objects are visible only because they send light to the eye, even dark ones scatter some light back.
activities.rationale: Asking about a dull black surface that the child can nevertheless SEE forces the contradiction that defeats 'only shiny things reflect': they can only see it because light bounced off it. The 'can you see it?' hook makes the reasoning hard to dodge; expect resistance and parallel school-versus-real-world explanations, so re-test.
sourceClaims: Common misconception that light is only reflected from shiny surfaces (e.g. mirrors) and that an object must either absorb OR reflect; the correct concept is that all objects absorb and reflect light to different degrees; the misconception is partly instruction-induced (always using mirror examples), so include shiny AND dull objects; conceptual change needs hands-on, repeated activities and is resistant.
learnerActions: Before switching on the torch in a dark room, predict: when I shine it on this dull black paper, will any light bounce off it and will you be able to see the paper? Say why first.
Shine the torch and observe whether you can see the paper.
Explain what the result shows about whether dull surfaces reflect light.
activities.intendedInsight: If you can see the surface of the dull black paper where the torch shines on it (not just a dark shape against a brighter background), light must have bounced off it into your eyes — so dull surfaces reflect some light too, not just shiny ones.

constraints: Always investigate BOTH shiny and dull/matt surfaces; restricting examples to mirrors is what breeds the 'only shiny things reflect' misconception.

Mastery at this age is the observational idea that light bounces off surfaces and that smooth shiny surfaces reflect best/most clearly — not the formal law of reflection (angle in = angle out), which is formalised later.
Avoid misleading analogies such as 'the Moon reflects like a mirror'; it reflects diffusely like a giant rock, not as an image-forming mirror.
Separate the special case of a shiny surface forming an image (seeing your face) from the general fact that every surface bounces some light; reflection happens even when no image forms.
Teach that surfaces usually both absorb and reflect light to different degrees; do not present absorbing and reflecting as a strict either/or.
A static labelled picture can introduce shiny/dull vocabulary but cannot show the beam bouncing or scattering, so it is a scaffold, not a substitute for the live beam comparison.

A sort/match/multiple-choice check (including a 'only shiny surfaces reflect' distractor) checks classification and the conclusion but does not itself elicit the physical bounce-and-compare experience; use it after the beam work, not instead of it.
How much light a dull or black surface returns depends on the material and setup; present the 'faint glow still reaches the target' as an outcome to test, not a guaranteed result for every surface.
Expect the corrected idea to be resistant; provide repeated hands-on, darkened-room experiences and re-test rather than assuming one demonstration fixes it.
A 3D mirror maze is engaging but a 2D bounce view reads the reflect-vs-scatter idea perfectly well at this age; 3D is optional, not required for the target insight.
Aim torch beams at targets, walls or surfaces for observation; do not direct a beam into eyes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source for the plane-mirror-first sequence and linking reflection to seeing (IOP Spark) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its specific recommendations as unconfirmed pending review.

The Beyond Penguins and NGSS 1-PS4-3 sources are marked verified:true in the row, but no source establishes comparative efficacy of any particular medium (2D interactive vs tactile vs quiz); such comparative claims have been softened to affordance/limit statements.

Self-audit: no arithmetic claims present. The physics retained (all surfaces reflect some light; shiny smooth surfaces reflect most cleanly; we see non-luminous objects by reflected light; black/dull surfaces still scatter some light; surfaces both absorb and reflect) is consistent with the sources and not overstated. Diffuse-vs-specular is kept observational for this age.

Reflectance of dull/black surfaces depends on material and setup; the 'faint glow still reaches the target' outcome is presented as an observation to test, not a guaranteed absolute result for every surface.

The 'object either absorbs OR reflects' misconception is surfaced in Activity 2 feedback and in the constraints, but there is no dedicated diagnostic item for it (as was also true of the original assessment); a reviewer may wish to add a targeted probe.

assess.poeTask: In a dark room, before switching on the torch, predict: when I shine it on this dull black paper, will you be able to see the paper — does any light bounce off it? Say why first. Then shine it and explain what the result shows.
probeDeeper: If the dull paper reflected NO light at all, could you see it in the dark room with just the torch? Why?
What's different about the way light bounces off a smooth mirror compared with the rough paper?
Name something dull that you can still see clearly right now — where is the light coming from that lets you see it?
assess.correctAnswer: Yes — light does bounce off the dull paper; that is the only reason you can see it. ALL surfaces reflect at least some light. Shiny smooth surfaces reflect it best and in a neat beam; dull rough ones scatter it, but they still bounce light back.

errorPatterns.pattern: Only shiny surfaces reflect: 'dull things don't reflect, only mirrors and shiny stuff do' — often 'reflection means a mirror image'
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is largely instruction-induced (all examples were mirrors) — deliberately investigate shiny AND dull surfaces; link 'you can see it' to 'light bounced off it'; expect resistance and parallel school-versus-real-world explanations.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — only shiny things like mirrors reflect light; the dull paper doesn't reflect any.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the dull black paper reflects no light at all

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflection = mirror image only: 'reflection is when you can see your face in it'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the special case (a shiny surface forming an image) from the general fact that every surface bounces light — reflection happens even when no image forms.
errorPatterns.distractor: Reflection only happens when you can see your face in something.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates reflection with seeing a picture of yourself; denies that plain bouncing counts as reflection

errorPatterns.pattern: Object is 'just its colour': we see the paper 'because it's black', not because light bounces off it
errorPatterns.nextMove: Connect back to how we see — objects are visible only because they send light to the eye; even a dark surface scatters some light back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains visibility by the object's colour rather than by reflected light reaching the eye

responseLevels.gap: Says only shiny things reflect and dull surfaces reflect nothing, or treats reflection as meaning a mirror image only.
responseLevels.full: States that all surfaces reflect some light (shiny best and neatest, dull scatter it) and uses this to explain how we can see a dull object, transferring the idea beyond mirrors.
responseLevels.partial: Knows shiny smooth surfaces reflect best and gives mirror/puddle examples, but still denies that dull surfaces reflect any light.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a dark room you shine a torch onto a piece of dull black sugar paper (not shiny at all). You can see the paper. Does ANY light bounce off it, or does light only bounce off shiny things like mirrors? Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: If every reflection example a child met was a mirror, they conclude 'only shiny things reflect'. Asking about a DULL black surface that they can nevertheless SEE forces the contradiction: they can only see it because light bounced off it into their eyes, so it must reflect. The 'can you see it?' hook makes the reasoning inescapable.
